lead.headline: Deadly Strike Hits Riyadh's Main Airport
lead.deck: Saudi authorities say an attack on the capital's international airport killed 12 people and wounded more than 300, raising fears that a regional conflict could spread further.
body: An airport is usually a place where people leave one country and arrive in another. On Saturday, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, became a scene of emergency evacuations after a missile strike. Saudi authorities said 12 people were killed and more than 300 were wounded.

The attack is part of a wider conflict involving Saudi Arabia, Yemen's Houthi movement and Iran. The Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen, have claimed attacks on Saudi infrastructure and say they are retaliating for Saudi actions. Saudi Arabia and its partners have blamed the Houthis, who receive support from Iran. In conflicts, responsibility for a particular strike can be disputed, so claims by each side need careful checking.

The airport matters beyond Riyadh. It connects Saudi Arabia to the world and carries business travellers, families, religious visitors and cargo. When a major airport is attacked, airlines may change routes, passengers can be stranded and governments must decide how to protect civilians without widening the fighting.

map.title: THE SOUTHERN GULF REGION
map.footnote: Schematic regional locator; not to scale
map.caption: Saudi Arabia borders Yemen to the south; the conflict's effects can travel far beyond the battlefield.

lead.why: The key idea is escalation: one attack can trigger retaliation, which can trigger another response. Saudi Arabia may seek help from allies, while the United States must weigh deterrence against the risk of being drawn deeper into the conflict. The region also sits near important shipping lanes and energy routes, so insecurity can affect fuel prices and goods far away. The reported death toll is serious, but the next question is whether leaders choose to widen the conflict or create room for diplomacy.

p1_stories.headline: Panama Faces a Long Aftershock Watch
p1_stories.deck: A powerful earthquake and continuing aftershocks have sent residents outdoors, damaged infrastructure and prompted emergency measures.
body: A powerful earthquake shook Panama on Friday, rattling buildings and sending people into streets and open spaces. Reports described a magnitude of 7.7, while later updates focused on aftershocks and damage in several communities. Authorities urged residents to be cautious around damaged buildings and coastal areas.

Earthquakes happen when stress built up along a fault is released suddenly, sending seismic waves through the ground. A magnitude number describes the size of the quake at its source; each whole-number increase represents a large jump in released energy. Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that follow the main event as the crust adjusts, and some can still be dangerous.

Panama is a narrow bridge of land between North and South America. It is also home to the Panama Canal, a major shipping shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. The canal was reported to remain operational in initial coverage, but emergency crews still have to check roads, utilities and buildings before everyday life can fully resume.

illustration.title: AFTER THE SHAKING
illustration.subtitle: Panama • Oct. 2026
illustration.caption: Aftershocks can continue after the main earthquake; damaged structures need careful inspection.

p1_stories.connect: The lesson from earthquakes is that preparedness matters before the ground moves. Building codes, emergency alerts, evacuation routes and practiced drills can reduce harm even when a quake cannot be predicted precisely. Panama's geography also matters: the canal is a global trade chokepoint, but the safety of people in nearby towns comes first. An infrastructure system can be important to the world and still depend on local roads, power, hospitals and rescue workers.

p2_stories.headline: Delhi Tightens Security Before Youth Protest
p2_stories.deck: Police detained more than 2,000 people and restricted parts of the capital ahead of a rally demanding answers about voter-list changes.
body: Parts of New Delhi were placed under heavy security on Saturday as authorities moved to stop a rally led by the youth group known as the Cockroach movement. Reuters reported that more than 2,000 people were detained and that some internet services and metro stations were disrupted.

The protest centres on revisions to voter lists overseen by India's Election Commission. Critics say the changes removed many names and could unfairly affect opposition voters; the government and election authorities reject allegations of wrongdoing. Those claims are politically consequential, but the precise effects and the reasons for individual removals require independent evidence.

Voter lists are the records that determine who can cast a ballot. Keeping them accurate is difficult in a large country where people move, turn 18, change addresses or die. The democratic test is whether the process is transparent, mistakes can be challenged, and eligible voters can get their names restored in time.
p2_stories.why: A democracy depends on more than holding an election. People also need confidence that the rules are fair, eligible voters can participate, and complaints can be reviewed independently. Authorities have a responsibility to keep public gatherings safe; protesters have rights to peaceful assembly and expression. The important questions are what evidence supports each side's claims, whether restrictions are proportionate, and whether the election process offers a credible way to resolve disputes.
also: The Reserve Bank of India raised its key policy rate to 5.5% on Oct. 7, its first increase in nearly four years, as inflation pressures grew.
Higher global energy prices can raise transport and manufacturing costs, which may eventually affect household budgets and the prices of goods.

p2_stories.headline: Storm Damage Leaves Communities Without Power
p2_stories.deck: Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Florida as a Category 2 storm before weakening, while heavy rain and wind continued to threaten parts of the Southeast.
body: Hurricane Isaias came ashore near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane, according to Associated Press reporting. It later weakened, but heavy rain, strong winds, fallen trees and power outages continued to affect communities across parts of the Southeast. At least four deaths were reported in early coverage.

A hurricane's category measures sustained wind speed, not every danger the storm brings. Even after winds weaken, rain can flood roads, trees can fall, and carbon monoxide from generators used indoors or too close to windows can be deadly. Local warnings can therefore remain important after a storm is downgraded.

The United States has emergency systems at federal, state and local levels. Federal disaster assistance can support response and recovery, but residents still depend on local utilities, emergency crews and neighbours. The first priorities are safety, reliable information and checking on people who may need help.

chart.title: HURRICANE CATEGORY SCALE
chart.subtitle: Saffir-Simpson wind categories (1–5)
chart.caption: Category measures sustained wind only; rainfall and storm surge can also be dangerous. Category 4 is shown for comparison, not as Isaias's category.

p2_stories.why: Extreme weather turns into a community emergency when hazards meet vulnerable people and infrastructure. Stronger building standards, reliable alerts, backup power for critical services and clear evacuation plans can reduce risk. Families should follow local emergency instructions and never run fuel-powered generators indoors. Climate change can increase the intensity of some heavy-rain events and raise coastal flood risk, but no single storm alone proves a long-term trend; scientists study many events and decades of data.
p2_stories.analyst: Think like an analyst: a storm's category describes wind, but a family's risk may depend more on flood depth, tree cover, housing quality or access to electricity. Which two local facts would you want before deciding whether a neighbourhood is safe?

briefs: Panama: Officials and residents are assessing damage and monitoring aftershocks following Friday's powerful earthquake.
Middle East: A reported drone strike in Sudan killed dozens of people near the Ethiopian border, according to Associated Press reporting.

vocab.def: A situation becoming more intense or dangerous. Today: leaders' responses to the Riyadh airport attack could widen or contain the conflict.
A smaller earthquake following a larger one as the ground adjusts. Today: Panama's communities are watching for more shaking.
The official list of people eligible to vote. Today: India's protest centres on disputed changes to voter lists.
The basic systems a society relies on, such as roads, power lines, airports and water networks. Today: storms and attacks can disrupt these systems.

learn.did_you_know: The Panama Canal lets ships travel between the Atlantic and Pacific without sailing all the way around South America. Its locks raise and lower ships between sea level and Gatun Lake, which sits above sea level. That makes the canal an engineering system as well as a geographic shortcut.
learn.quote: A useful question in a crisis is not only 'What happened?' but also 'What do we know, and how do we know it?'

sports.title: Sports desk: separate the result from the noise
sports.body: A good sports report distinguishes the final score from the reasons behind it: injuries, tactics, conditions and decisions can all matter. Before sharing a breaking result, check the competition's official site and at least one reliable report.

watchlist: Whether Saudi Arabia and its partners announce a response to the Riyadh airport attack, and whether diplomatic channels remain open.
Whether Panama's aftershock assessments change the picture of damage, and whether emergency services report new safety risks.
